title: “ALL SCRIPTURE IS GOD-BREATHED” — BUT WHICH SCRIPTURES WAS PAUL ACTUALLY TALKING ABOUT?
paragraphs: “ALL SCRIPTURE IS GOD-BREATHED” — BUT WHICH SCRIPTURES WAS PAUL ACTUALLY TALKING ABOUT?

The answer may challenge what you have always assumed about the Bible, take you back to the Scriptures Jesus Himself treasured, and reveal why the Word of God was never meant merely to fill your mind—but to lead your broken heart to the Savior who can rewrite your story.
What if one of the most quoted verses about the Bible is also one of the most frequently misunderstood?
You have probably heard it preached.
You may have memorized it as a child.
You may even have used it to defend your faith.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God…”
Second Timothy 3:16.
A familiar verse. A powerful declaration. A foundation for Christian confidence in the authority of Scripture.
But there is a question many believers have never stopped long enough to ask.
When Paul wrote those words, what Scriptures was he actually talking about?
Because when Paul wrote his letter to Timothy, the twenty-seven books we now recognize as the New Testament had not yet been gathered into a completed collection.
The four Gospels had not yet been assembled alongside Acts, the apostolic letters, and Revelation into the New Testament canon we recognize today.
Some New Testament writings were already circulating among Christian communities. Others were written later, depending on the dating of the individual books.
And the complete Bible you carry today—with its Old Testament and New Testament bound together—did not yet exist in that form.
So what did Paul mean?
Was he referring only to the Old Testament?
Was he anticipating the New Testament?
Does his statement establish the inspiration of every book in our Bible?
And perhaps the most important question of all:
If Scripture is truly breathed out by God, why do so many people who know its verses still live as though they have never encountered its Author?
Stay with me.
Because this is not merely a conversation about ancient manuscripts, Greek vocabulary, or the history of the biblical canon.
This is about the voice of God breaking through centuries of human confusion.
It is about the Scriptures that led a young man named Timothy toward salvation.
It is about the Bible Jesus read, the promises Jesus fulfilled, and the truth that no amount of religious knowledge can replace a living relationship with Jesus Christ.
And somewhere in this story, you may discover that the question is not simply whether you believe the Bible came from God.
The question is whether you are allowing the God who speaks through Scripture to change your life.
Paul wrote to Timothy:

“And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:”
—2 Timothy 3:15–16, KJV
Notice something extraordinary.
Before Paul says that Scripture is inspired by God, he reminds Timothy that he has known the sacred writings since childhood.
That detail matters more than many people realize.
Timothy was not raised with a leather-bound King James Bible on his bedside table.
He did not grow up flipping through Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Romans, and Revelation as one completed New Testament.
He grew up with the sacred writings of Israel.
Paul had already mentioned Timothy's sincere faith and the influence of his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice in 2 Timothy 1:5.
Acts 16:1 also tells us that Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer, while his father was Greek.
The Scriptures Timothy knew from childhood were therefore the Jewish sacred Scriptures—the writings Christians now call the Old Testament.
The Law.
The Prophets.
The Psalms and the other sacred writings.
The accounts of creation, the fall, the flood, the covenant with Abraham, the exodus from Egypt, the kingdom of David, the warnings of the prophets, and the promises of a coming Redeemer.
These were the writings that formed the spiritual world in which Timothy was raised.
These were the Scriptures Paul explicitly identified as able to make Timothy wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
And that should stop us in our tracks.
Because Paul was not telling Timothy that the Old Testament was an outdated religious collection that Christians could safely ignore.
He was saying that these ancient writings possessed the power to make someone wise concerning salvation in Jesus Christ.
Not salvation apart from Christ.
Not salvation through keeping the Law perfectly.
Not salvation through ethnic identity, religious performance, or human righteousness.
Salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
Think about that.
The Scriptures written centuries before Bethlehem were already preparing people to recognize the One who would be born there.
The writings that spoke of sacrifices were preparing hearts for the Lamb of God.
The promises made to Abraham were pointing toward a blessing that would reach the nations.
The covenant with David was preparing Israel for a King whose kingdom would endure.
The prophets were announcing judgment against sin while holding out hope for restoration, forgiveness, and a new covenant.
And Paul was telling Timothy that these sacred writings were not disconnected religious artifacts.
They belonged to the unfolding story of God's redemption.
But now we must look even closer.
Because the original Greek text makes Paul's statement especially remarkable.
Second Timothy 3:16 begins:
Πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος
Transliterated:
Pasa graphē theopneustos kai ōphelimos.
A natural translation is:
“Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable.”
The King James Version renders the verse:
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable…”
The central word is θεόπνευστος — theopneustos.
It combines theos, meaning God, with a word element associated with breathing.
The term means “God-breathed” or “inspired by God.”
Paul was not merely describing Scripture as emotionally uplifting, intellectually impressive, or spiritually meaningful.
He was identifying its divine origin.
The expression does not mean that biblical writers simply experienced the same kind of inspiration a poet might feel while watching a sunset.
It speaks of Scripture as originating from God.
The Bible's own account of inspiration also recognizes that God spoke through human beings.
Second Peter 1:21 says:
“For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.”
The Greek verb translated “moved” is pheromenoi, carrying the idea of being borne or carried along.
The biblical writers were real people.
They wrote in recognizable languages, historical settings, literary styles, and circumstances.
Moses did not write exactly like David.
Isaiah did not write exactly like Amos.
Luke did not write exactly like Paul.
And John did not write exactly like James.
Yet the Christian doctrine of inspiration affirms that God worked through these human authors so that their writings communicate what He intended.
Divine inspiration does not erase the human dimensions of Scripture.
It explains why Christians receive these writings as more than merely human testimony.
There is also a translation question worth understanding.

Because ancient Greek manuscripts did not have the same punctuation conventions as modern English Bibles, and because the Greek wording contains no explicit verb corresponding to “is,” interpreters have discussed whether the phrase should be rendered “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable” or “Every God-breathed Scripture is also profitable.”
The first reading has been widely accepted and is reflected in many major translations.
The second is grammatically possible, although it is less commonly preferred.
This distinction matters when studying the verse carefully, but it does not change the larger context: Paul is affirming the divine character and practical usefulness of the sacred writings.
And look at what those writings are profitable for.
Teaching.
Reproof.
Correction.
Training in righteousness.
Not merely winning arguments.
Not collecting theological facts to impress other Christians.
Not building a reputation as someone who knows more verses than everyone else.
Scripture teaches us what is true.
It confronts us when we are wrong.
It calls us back when we wander.
It trains us to live in a manner pleasing to God.
And the next verse explains the purpose:
“That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.”
—2 Timothy 3:17, KJV
The word translated “perfect” here carries the sense of being capable, complete, or adequately equipped, not of achieving sinless perfection by human effort.
God's Word is intended to shape God's people for faithful living.
That means the Bible is not merely something you study.
It is something God uses to examine you.
And sometimes that examination hurts.
Because it is possible to know the language of grace while refusing to forgive someone.
It is possible to defend biblical marriage while secretly nurturing lust.
It is possible to preach generosity while being controlled by greed.
It is possible to quote verses about humility while craving applause.
It is possible to speak about repentance while protecting the very sin God is calling you to surrender.
You can know the correct Greek pronunciation of theopneustos and still refuse to obey the plain teaching of Jesus.
You can own ten Bibles and never allow one of them to confront your pride.
You can spend years defending the authority of Scripture while quietly resisting its authority over your own heart.
And that is where this ancient passage becomes painfully personal.
The tragedy is not simply that some people reject the Bible. It is that some people defend the Bible while refusing to let its truth correct them.
But there is another question we must answer.
If Paul was referring to the sacred writings Timothy knew from childhood, does that mean 2 Timothy 3:16 applies only to the Old Testament?
Here we must be careful.
We should not force Paul to say something his immediate context does not establish.
But neither should we ignore what the rest of the New Testament says about apostolic teaching and Scripture.
The clearest historical starting point is this: the sacred writings Timothy knew from childhood were the Jewish Scriptures.
That is the immediate reference in verse 15.
When Paul continues in verse 16 with the broader expression “all Scripture” or “every Scripture,” he makes a general statement about writings that belong to the category of Scripture.
His wording does not provide a complete list of which books belong in that category.
Nor does it establish that Paul was referring to every one of the twenty-seven New Testament books in their final canonical collection.
That collection had not yet been completed.
However, the New Testament itself gives evidence that apostolic writings were already being treated with exceptional authority, and in some cases associated with Scripture.
Consider 1 Timothy 5:18.
Paul writes:
The first statement comes from Deuteronomy 25:4.
The second closely matches Jesus' words recorded in Luke 10:7.
This is significant.
Paul introduces the sayings with the expression “the Scripture says.”
Many interpreters understand this as evidence that Jesus' teaching, in a form corresponding to Luke's Gospel, was being cited alongside the Law as Scripture.
Others caution that this verse alone cannot prove Paul was quoting a completed written Gospel of Luke rather than a circulating tradition of Jesus' teaching.
That historical qualification is important.
But either way, the verse demonstrates that authoritative teaching from Jesus was central to the early Christian community.
Now consider another remarkable passage.
Second Peter 3:15–16 refers to Paul's letters and acknowledges that some things in them are difficult to understand.
Then Peter warns about people who distort these writings:
“...as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.”
The phrase “the other scriptures” strongly suggests that Paul's letters were being placed in the category of Scripture.
That is an important piece of evidence for the recognition of apostolic writings as scriptural.
There is a historical discussion concerning the authorship and dating of 2 Peter, and scholars do not all agree about those questions.
Nevertheless, the passage as it stands in the New Testament bears witness to the recognition of Paul's letters as authoritative Scripture.
We should also remember what Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 14:37:
“...the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord.”
Paul understood his apostolic instruction as carrying authority derived from Christ.
And Jesus Himself prepared His apostles for their witness.
In John 14:26, He promised that the Holy Spirit would teach them and bring His words to their remembrance.
In John 16:13, He spoke of the Spirit guiding them into truth.

These promises belong first to the apostolic setting in which Jesus spoke them. They should not be casually turned into a guarantee that every private impression a modern believer experiences is divine revelation.
Together, these passages help explain why the early church received apostolic teaching with such seriousness.
The church did not begin with a completed New Testament table of contents.
It began with the risen Christ, the testimony of His apostles, the proclamation of the Gospel, and the Scriptures of Israel.
The apostolic writings were produced, circulated, read, preserved, and eventually recognized together as the New Testament canon.
Christians differ in their accounts of the precise historical process of canon recognition and in some Old Testament canonical boundaries.
But one distinction remains essential:
Second Timothy 3:16 teaches the God-breathed character of Scripture. It does not, by itself, provide a table of contents for the Christian Bible.
To establish which books belong in the canon, Christians must consider the broader biblical witness and the historical reception of these writings.
That is not a weakness in Scripture.
It is simply the difference between asking what Scripture is and asking which writings belong to Scripture.
Confusing those questions creates unnecessary arguments.
Distinguishing them allows us to read Paul more faithfully.
And here is something else we must never overlook.

When we say the Old Testament was Scripture for Jesus and the apostles, we must not imagine that every ancient Jewish community possessed an identical physical collection arranged exactly like a modern Protestant Old Testament.
The Hebrew Scriptures were commonly understood in broad divisions such as the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings.
Jewish communities also used Greek translations of sacred writings, especially in Greek-speaking settings.
The Septuagint—the ancient Greek translation tradition of the Jewish Scriptures—played a major role in the biblical world of early Christianity.
The contents and boundaries of ancient Greek biblical manuscript collections were not entirely uniform, and later Christian traditions came to differ concerning certain Old Testament books.
Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox Christians therefore do not have identical Old Testament canons.
These historical realities should make us more careful, not less confident in Christ.
Paul's central concern in 2 Timothy 3 was not to settle every later canonical disagreement.
He wanted Timothy to remain faithful to the sacred writings that testified to salvation through Jesus Christ.
And now we reach something even more beautiful.
Because long before Paul wrote to Timothy, Jesus Himself explained how the Scriptures pointed toward Him.
After His resurrection, two disciples were walking toward Emmaus.
Their hopes had been shattered.
The One they believed would redeem Israel had been crucified.
They had heard reports of an empty tomb, but their hearts were still clouded by confusion.
They were walking beside the risen Christ without recognizing Him.
Imagine that.
The answer to their grief was already walking beside them.
The Savior they thought they had lost was listening to their sorrow.
And Luke tells us:
“And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.”
—Luke 24:27, KJV
Did you catch that?
Jesus began with Moses and the Prophets.
He explained the Scriptures in relation to Himself.
He did not treat the Old Testament as a failed religious experiment that had become irrelevant.
He revealed how its story reached its fulfillment in Him.
Later, in Luke 24:44, Jesus spoke of the things written concerning Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
These expressions point to the sacred writings of Israel.
And Jesus declared that what had been written concerning Him must be fulfilled.
The Old Testament is not a collection of random stories with Jesus artificially inserted into every detail.
Responsible interpretation still requires attention to each passage's original context, literary form, and historical meaning.
Not every object, number, or event should be turned into a secret symbol of Christ.
But the great redemptive story of Scripture genuinely moves toward Him.
Creation reveals the goodness of God and the tragedy of human rebellion.
The covenant promises establish the hope of blessing and redemption.
The sacrificial system teaches the seriousness of sin and the need for atonement.
The prophets announce both judgment and restoration.
The promises of a coming king, servant, and new covenant find their fulfillment in Jesus.
And the New Testament proclaims that the crucified and risen Christ is the center of God's saving purpose.
This is why John the Baptist could look at Jesus and declare:
“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.”
—John 1:29, KJV
This is why Paul could write:
—Romans 10:4, KJV
The Greek word translated “end” is telos, a word that can express an end, goal, or culmination.
Christ is the culmination toward which the Law's saving significance points. He is not permission to abandon God's righteousness or disregard the moral demands of discipleship.
He is the One in whom the promises of redemption reach their fulfillment.
And suddenly the question about 2 Timothy 3:16 becomes more than a historical curiosity.
Because the Scriptures Paul was talking about were the very writings that prepared the world for Jesus.
They told the story of humanity's fall.
They revealed the holiness of God.
They exposed the seriousness of sin.
They carried the promises of mercy.
And they pointed toward the Savior who would enter our broken world to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
This is the Gospel.
Not that humanity climbed high enough to reach God.
But that God, in His mercy, came to save sinners through His Son.
Not that we repaired ourselves until we became worthy of forgiveness.
But that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures.
Paul himself summarized that message in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
“...Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.”
Notice the repetition.
According to the Scriptures.
The Gospel did not appear as an afterthought.
The death and resurrection of Jesus belong to the fulfillment of God's redemptive plan.
And this matters deeply for anyone who has ever wondered whether God could still redeem a ruined life.
Maybe you have made decisions you wish you could erase.
Maybe you have hidden sins behind a respectable Christian appearance.
Maybe you have wounded someone who trusted you.
Maybe you have spent years trying to convince people that you are spiritually stronger than you actually are.
Maybe you have opened your Bible with a heavy heart, knowing exactly what it says about righteousness, yet feeling painfully aware of how far you have fallen.
And somewhere inside, a question keeps returning.
Can God still want someone like me?
Listen carefully.
The Bible does not minimize your sin to make you feel better.
It tells the truth.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
But the same Gospel that exposes your sin also announces the grace of God.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we proved that we would never fail again.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
The Gospel calls us to turn from sin and trust the Savior.
It does not offer cheap reassurance that allows us to remain comfortably enslaved to what destroys us.
Grace forgives.
Grace also teaches us to renounce ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
And that is why Scripture's work of correction is not the enemy of God's love.
It is one of the ways God calls His children back to truth.
Sometimes the verse that exposes you is the verse God uses to begin restoring you.
Sometimes the passage you would rather avoid is precisely the passage you need to read.
Sometimes conviction is the doorway through which repentance enters.
And sometimes the most merciful thing God does is refuse to let you remain comfortable in a lie.
Consider David.
A king.
A worshiper.
A man who wrote psalms.
And yet a man who committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged the death of Uriah.
His position did not excuse his sin.
His spiritual history did not make his actions harmless.
And when the prophet Nathan confronted him, the truth could no longer be hidden behind royal authority.
David's response in 2 Samuel 12:13 was simple:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Psalm 51 gives us a profound picture of repentance associated with that terrible failure.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
—Psalm 51:10, KJV
David could not undo Uriah's death.
Forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence of his actions.
But his sin did not place him beyond the reach of God's mercy.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ would come from David's royal line.
Not because David's wickedness was good.
Not because the victims of sin were unimportant.
But because God's redemptive purposes are greater than human failure.
That is the heartbeat of our message:
But understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
He does not call evil good.
He does not excuse betrayal, abuse, dishonesty, or injustice.
He brings sinners to repentance.
He offers forgiveness through His blood.
He creates new life where sin once ruled.
He teaches the redeemed to walk in truth, humility, restitution where appropriate, and obedience.
The Gospel is not the cancellation of accountability.
It is the triumph of God's grace over the guilt and dominion of sin through Jesus Christ.
And the Scriptures bear witness to that Savior.
This is why Jesus spoke such sobering words to religious people who searched the Scriptures diligently.
In John 5:39–40, He said:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.”
Consider the tragedy.
They studied the sacred writings.
They valued religious knowledge.
They believed they possessed the truth.
Yet they refused to come to the very One to whom those Scriptures testified.
It is possible to hold the written testimony in your hands while resisting the Savior it reveals.
That should humble every one of us.
Including the person writing this.
Including the person reading it.
Because we can become so busy discussing biblical authority that we forget the purpose of biblical revelation.
We can argue about manuscripts while neglecting mercy.
We can debate translations while refusing reconciliation.
We can identify false teaching in others while excusing the sin in ourselves.
We can become experts at explaining the Scriptures without becoming faithful disciples of Jesus.
And none of that is what Paul wanted for Timothy.
Paul did not tell him to continue in the sacred writings so that he could become arrogant.
He told him to continue in what he had learned.
He reminded him of the Scriptures that lead to salvation through Christ.
He explained that Scripture teaches, reproves, corrects, and trains.
And he emphasized that God's servant should be equipped for every good work.
The goal was never merely information.
It was faithful formation in the truth of God.
That brings us to another important point.
When Christians say that Scripture is inspired, they must still interpret it responsibly.
A verse removed from its context can be used to support an idea the biblical author never intended.
A promise made to a particular person in a particular historical setting should not automatically be turned into an unconditional promise to every modern reader.
Poetry must be read as poetry.
Historical narrative must be understood as narrative.
Prophecy must be studied with attention to its original audience and fulfillment.
Letters must be read in light of their occasion and argument.
And the Bible must be interpreted in a way that honors the unity of God's revelation without flattening the differences between its books.
The original Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek can help us understand important details.
Most of the Old Testament was written in Hebrew, with certain portions in Aramaic.
The New Testament was written in Koine Greek.
Studying these languages can illuminate the meaning of biblical expressions.
But knowing an original-language word does not automatically make an interpretation correct.
Context still matters.
Grammar matters.
Literary form matters.
Historical setting matters.
And the broader biblical witness matters.
There is no spiritual advantage in using impressive Greek words to support an interpretation the passage does not actually teach.
God's Word deserves more reverence than that.
For example, the Hebrew expression often translated “word of the LORD” is:
דְּבַר־יְהוָה
Devar-YHWH.
It means “word of the LORD.”
The expression appears throughout the Hebrew Scriptures in contexts where God communicates His message, often through His prophets.
But it would be careless to claim that every occurrence of this phrase directly means the completed Christian Bible.
That would ignore the specific contexts in which the expression appears.
Likewise, the Greek term graphē, meaning “writing” or “Scripture,” must be understood according to its usage.
In New Testament contexts, it commonly refers to sacred Scripture.
But the word itself does not magically supply a list of canonical books.
The context tells us how it is being used.
This is why honest biblical interpretation is so important.
We do not honor Scripture by making it say more than it says.
We honor Scripture by listening carefully to what God has actually communicated through it.
And the more carefully we listen, the more clearly we see Jesus.
The Scriptures tell us that we were created for God.
That sin has separated humanity from Him.
That no human effort can erase our guilt.
That God's promises are trustworthy.
That Christ fulfilled the Scriptures through His life, death, and resurrection.
That forgiveness is offered through Him.
And that those who belong to Him are called into a transformed life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that believers will never struggle again.
It is a declaration of new identity and new life in Christ.
The Christian life still involves repentance, perseverance, sanctification, and dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But the person who belongs to Jesus is no longer defined ultimately by the condemnation of sin.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to remember today.
You have been carrying your past like a sentence that can never be overturned.
You have been replaying the same mistake.
The same shame.
The same words you wish you had never spoken.
The same moment when everything seemed to fall apart.
And you wonder whether God has finally grown tired of hearing you ask for forgiveness.
Do not confuse the seriousness of your sin with the insufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
His blood is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not permission to keep practicing deception.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
And if you have been wounded by someone else's sin, hear this too.
The Gospel does not require you to deny what happened.
It does not demand that you pretend the damage was small.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical, and rebuilding trust may require time, truth, safety, and genuine change.
God's grace does not trivialize the suffering of victims.
The Savior who bore our sins also cares about justice and truth.
That is part of what makes the Gospel so beautiful.
It does not have to lie about human brokenness in order to announce divine hope.
Now return to the original question.
What Scripture was Paul referring to when he wrote that all Scripture is God-breathed?
Most directly, the sacred writings of Israel that Timothy had known since childhood—the Scriptures Christians call the Old Testament.
That is the clearest conclusion from the immediate context.
But Paul's broader statement about Scripture's divine origin is not a declaration that God could never inspire further apostolic writings.
The New Testament provides evidence of the authority of apostolic teaching and of the recognition of certain apostolic writings as Scripture.
Christians therefore understand 2 Timothy 3:16 as expressing a principle about the nature of Scripture that applies to the writings they receive as the completed biblical canon.
That application must be supported by the broader biblical and historical case for the canon, not by pretending that Timothy possessed a completed New Testament as a child.
We do not need to rewrite history to defend the Bible.
We do not need to invent facts to honor God.
We do not need to conceal difficult questions to preserve faith.
Truth does not become stronger when we exaggerate it.
And reverence for Scripture should make us more committed to accuracy, not less.
The same Paul who spoke of God-breathed Scripture also called Timothy to handle the word of truth rightly.
Second Timothy 2:15 says:
“Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.”
The Greek expression translated “rightly dividing” is orthotomounta, conveying the idea of handling or guiding something correctly.
The point is faithful treatment of the truth.
Not manipulating verses.
Not forcing conclusions.
Not twisting the text to protect a favorite tradition.
But handling God's Word with integrity.
And that is the kind of discipleship we need today.
Not shallow religious excitement that disappears the moment life becomes difficult.
Not endless arguments that produce pride instead of holiness.
Not motivational messages that use the name of Jesus while avoiding His call to repentance.
We need Scripture.
We need sound doctrine.
We need the Gospel.
We need prayer.
We need Christian fellowship.
We need correction when we wander.
We need encouragement when we are weary.
And above all, we need Jesus Christ.
Because even the most carefully preserved Bible cannot save someone who refuses the Savior it proclaims.
The written Word bears witness to the living Christ.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us…”
The Greek expression is:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
In John's Gospel, ho Logos refers to the eternal Word who was with God and was God, as John 1:1 declares.
John is not simply saying that a physical book became a human being.
He is proclaiming the incarnation of the eternal Son.
Jesus Christ entered human history.
He lived among us.
He revealed the Father.
He died for sinners.
And He rose victorious over death.
The Scriptures testify to Him, but they are not interchangeable with His person.
The Bible is God's inspired written revelation.
Jesus is the incarnate Son of God.
We honor the Scriptures precisely because they truthfully reveal the Savior.
And when we read them rightly, we do not stop at admiration for ancient words.
We are called to respond to the Christ they proclaim.
So what should you do with this truth?
Perhaps the answer is simpler—and more demanding—than you expected.
Open your Bible again.
Not merely to prove somebody wrong.
Not merely to prepare another social media argument.
Not merely to find a verse that confirms what you already want to believe.
Open it with humility.
Read the passage in context.
Ask what the author was communicating.
Consider how it fits within God's unfolding revelation.
Look for what it teaches about His character, His holiness, His mercy, and His redemptive purposes.
And when Scripture confronts a sin you have been defending, do not immediately look for an excuse.
Bring it before the Lord.
When it exposes bitterness, seek grace to forgive.
When it reveals pride, humble yourself.
When it corrects false beliefs, be willing to learn.
When it points you toward Christ, trust Him.
When it commands obedience, do not be satisfied with admiration.
Ask God to make you a doer of His Word.
Because a Bible that remains closed cannot instruct you.
A verse that is constantly twisted cannot correct you.
And truth that is endlessly admired but deliberately disobeyed will not produce the faithful life Paul described.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to compete with the authority of Scripture.
Not to make any human ministry the center of your faith.
But to keep directing people toward Jesus Christ through biblical truth, repentance, grace, encouragement, and discipleship.
We want to reach the person who has stopped reading the Bible because life became painful.
The believer who is struggling quietly.
The parent praying for a wandering child.
The young Christian trying to distinguish truth from spiritual confusion.
The person who has heard about Jesus but has never understood the Gospel.
The one who is ashamed of the past.
The one who is tempted to give up.
And the one who is spiritually comfortable but desperately needs to wake up.
We believe biblical nourishment should reach people who may not be able to afford a shelf full of Christian books.
And we believe that growing in Christ should involve more than consuming an inspiring post and forgetting it an hour later.
It should lead to Scripture reading, prayer, repentance, Christian community, and daily obedience to Jesus.
It helps sustain the labor involved in producing teaching materials and making free resources available to more people.
But we want to be clear about something important.
Christians hold differing convictions about how Old Testament tithing applies under the new covenant, but the New Testament clearly teaches willing, generous giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
God is not honored by financial pressure disguised as spiritual obligation.
He is honored by sincere faith, obedience, love, and generosity.
And you do not have to purchase anything to receive the grace of Jesus Christ.

But if this ministry has strengthened your faith, and you have the ability and desire to help it reach others, your voluntary support can become a meaningful act of partnership in Gospel-centered work.
Those items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
You can still help this message reach people.
Someone may be carrying a burden of guilt.
Someone may have walked away from church after encountering shallow teaching.
Someone may be waiting for an explanation of Scripture that is both honest and centered on Jesus.
You may never know who needed to read this today.
And invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who do not yet believe to follow as well.
Not because following a page makes someone a disciple.
But because a faithful message can become one more opportunity for someone to encounter the truth of God's Word.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something more personal than a question about the biblical canon.
When was the last time you allowed Scripture to correct something in your life that you did not want to surrender?
Not somebody else's sin.
Not a false teaching you spotted online.
Not a theological argument you won.
Something in your own heart.
A resentment.
A secret compromise.
A prideful attitude.
A refusal to forgive.
A habit you have been hiding.
A fear that keeps you from trusting God.
Be honest.
If the Word of God has been exposing something in your life, you do not need to pretend you are already perfect.
Someone else may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Jesus Christ still transforms lives.
You do not have to disclose private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
A sincere word of faith may be enough to encourage another believer.
Because this is what makes the truth of 2 Timothy so extraordinary.
Paul was writing to a young servant of Christ, reminding him to remain grounded in the Scriptures he had known since childhood.
Those Scriptures were not given to entertain him.
They were not given to make him feel superior.
They were not given so that he could become skilled at religious arguments while neglecting righteousness.
They were God-breathed writings, profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training.
And they were able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, that same truth confronts us.
The Bible is not an accessory to the Christian life.
It is not a decorative object for the coffee table.
It is not a collection of inspirational phrases to use whenever we need emotional comfort.
It is sacred revelation that calls us to know God truthfully and respond to Him faithfully.
And at the center of its saving message stands Jesus Christ.
The One promised.
The One crucified.
The One risen.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who will return.
The One who is worthy of every act of obedience, every sacrifice of love, and every genuine expression of worship.
So yes, ask which Scriptures Paul meant.
Study the historical context.
Learn the Greek.
Understand the canon.
Examine the evidence.
Do not be afraid of difficult questions.
But when you have finished asking what Paul meant by “All Scripture is God-breathed,” do not walk away without asking what those Scriptures are calling you to do.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you misunderstood a verse.
It would be spending your life studying the Scriptures that testify of Jesus while never surrendering your heart to Him.
The Bible you have been trying so hard to understand has been pointing you all along to the Savior who already knows everything about you—and still calls you to come to Him.
